key_insight: At reduced rutile TiO2(110) surfaces, small-polaron motion is dramatically slower than in bulk because surface geometry removes efficient hopping paths and confines electrons to a few near-surface trajectories.
engineering_relevance: This helps explain lower electron mobility in porous rutile TiO2 and informs surface/defect engineering for oxide-based catalysis, photovoltaics, and energy-storage devices.
method: Machine-learning-accelerated polaron dynamics was extended from bulk oxides to a redox-active oxide surface.
Several nanoseconds of finite-temperature dynamics were sampled across a temperature range.
Oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110) was used as the model system to resolve hopping pathways and vacancy effects.
evidence_signal: The study combines long-timescale simulations with temperature-dependent sampling to show orders-of-magnitude mobility suppression and to map preferred hopping and vacancy-bound electron configurations.
watch_item: The conclusions are drawn for a specific reduced surface model, so transferability to other oxide orientations, defect concentrations, or adsorbate conditions should be validated.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
